description.value: This study examined neural responses to smoking and food cues, functional connectivity during cue presentation, and relationships between cue reactivity, connectivity, and nicotine dependence severity in smokers.

value: We hypothesized that smoking cues would elicit greater neural responses in the ACC, OFC, insula, dorsal and ventral striatum than normal appetitive cues and that increased dependence would be associated with an increased difference in these regions.

In addition, we hypothesized that functional connectivity during smoking cues as compared with food cues between insula and dACC would be stronger in individuals who were more severely nicotine dependent.

value: Smoking videos elicited greater response than food videos in bilateral orbitofrontal cortex, medial frontal gyrus/supplementary motor area, middle frontal gyrus, inferior parietal lobe, and middle temporal gyrus. Only the bilateral orbitofrontal cortex, bilateral inferior parietal lobe, and supplementary motor area showed significant increases above baseline during smoking videos; the other differences reflected less deactivation below baseline compared with food videos.
These results suggest that smokers engage attentional networks and default mode networks involved in self-referential processing to a greater degree during smoking cues.

value: Food videos elicited greater response than smoking videos in the bilateral visual cortex, inferior parietal cortex, pre/post-central gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, frontal pole, and striatum.

All differences were the result of food videos eliciting responses above baseline to a greater degree than smoking videos; in no case was the significant difference the result of reduced deactivation below baseline.

spans.text: The cue-exposure task consisted of two 6-min runs with pseudorandom presentations of seven different smoking-related videos and seven different food-related videos.

description.value: Participants viewed 14 smoking-related videos across two 6-minute runs. Videos depicted preparation of cigarettes for subsequent ingestion and the act of smoking; each video lasted 7–14 seconds. No participant response was required.

Participants viewed 14 food-related videos across two 6-minute runs. Videos depicted preparation of food for subsequent ingestion and the act of ingestion; each video lasted 7–14 seconds. No participant response was required.
